summary: Pico Peak's lookout: a 1914 wood tower, a 1925 steel replacement, then dismantled and re-erected on Killington in 1963 or 1964.

facts.design: Steel tower (1925) with Aermotor parts, replacing a wood tower condemned as unsafe
facts.status_note: Dismantled and re-erected on Killington Peak in 1963 or 1964; no tower is described on Pico Peak today.

access.note: The summit is reached by the 0.4-mile Pico Link Trail; the ski area is part of Killington Resort. No source describes summit restrictions.

visit.trail_note: The summit is reached by the 0.4-mile Pico Link Trail.

events.note: Proctor paid for a tower, cabin and telephone line on the mountain; the 1914 entry calls Pico a lookout point
Tower turned over to the Forest Service for use as a fire lookout station

Dana Rowe named as the look-out man for the new tower
Someone deliberately smashed nearly all the glass in the windows at the top of the tower

Dismantled at Pico and re-erected on Killington summit; state report cites lease difficulty. WillhiteWeb gives 1963; Forest Lookouts covers 1963-64

notes_for_editor: Record height 6.1 m (20 ft) matches the wood tower condemned in 1925; the planned steel replacement was 35 ft (about 10.7 m). height_m was left out of facts because the sources disagree on which structure was measured. Forest Lookouts repeats the 1925 condemnation text under May 24, 1950; treated here as a repeat, since no other source describes a second rebuild. The 1963-64 state report says the moved tower was 'installed on Pico about 1914', which does not fit the 1925 steel replacement; the sources do not show which structure went to Killington. The Killington story says the tower was 'first built on Pico Peak in about 1920'; the Pico sources date the first tower to 1914, so the Killington story's date may need a look. The record's design (Aermotor) and material (steel) are supported by the 1925 newspaper. No source describes what remains on the Pico summit. The 1984 Killington event is included only as the moved tower's later history and is not a Pico fact.
